findings.title: Reconcile can declare a running mutation not applied
findings.why_it_matters: After a mutation times out or loses its reply, reconcile can return not_applied and arm a retry while the original mutation is still queued or executing; the first mutation can subsequently land. The engine continues handling the original connection after the adapter drops it, and its content reads do not take the mutation lock, so a point-in-time content comparison cannot establish the operation's final outcome. A durable operation identifier and an engine-side final-status/barrier check are needed before returning a definitive result.
findings.suggested_fix: Assign mutations durable request IDs and reconcile their final engine-side status after the mutation pipeline has finished; until then return an explicitly unknown outcome rather than not_applied or a retry-ready ledger entry.

findings.title: Unreadable files reconcile as successfully deleted
findings.why_it_matters: A delete with a lost reply can be reported as applied even though the file still exists but cannot be read, or now contains invalid UTF-8. The content read collapses every filesystem read error and UTF-8 failure to null, and reconcile interprets null as proof of absence. Distinguishing a confirmed not-found result from other failures prevents this false success.
findings.suggested_fix: Return null only for a confirmed NotFound; propagate permission, I/O, and UTF-8 errors through the content wire response so reconcile leaves the outcome unknown.

findings.title: Mutation preflight reads can block the mutation slot forever
findings.why_it_matters: If the engine accepts a connection but stops answering, a rename-type request can hang indefinitely while holding the adapter's only mutation permit, so every later mutation is rejected until the process is restarted. The 30-second timeout is applied only to the eventual mutation exchange, not the type and cascade preflight reads; ordinary file mutation editability and create preflights also use unbounded reads. Bounding the preflight exchanges releases capacity and returns a definite no-write error.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply the existing read deadline to every engine read in mutation preflight, including type/cascade, member resolution, and create absence checks, and ensure the held permit is released on timeout.

findings.title: Internal stdio rejections bypass backpressure accounting
findings.why_it_matters: A client that stops draining stdout after sending repeated rejected versioned pings can leave the MCP process hung indefinitely, despite the promised five-second outbound timeout. The receive loop sends those rejections directly into the queue without consuming a slot or applying the timeout, and the writer nevertheless adds a slot for each one; the accounting can also grow beyond its intended bound. Route every response through the same permit and timeout path so saturation closes the connection.
findings.suggested_fix: Account for a slot for every internally generated rejection and bound queue insertion by outbound_wait, sharing the same send/backpressure logic as ordinary responses.

findings.title: Adapter installer requires an ignored target symlink
findings.why_it_matters: On a clean checkout the adapter installer builds successfully but fails to install because it looks under tb-mcp-rs/target, which is ignored and is not created by Cargo configured to use the monorepo .cargo-target directory. The local symlink relied on by this script is not tracked. Resolve Cargo's target directory as the root installer does instead of relying on a machine-local symlink.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve target_directory with cargo metadata after configuring the toolchain, matching the root install.sh, and install the release binary from that directory.

findings.title: Force stop can kill an unrelated reused PID
findings.why_it_matters: After a daemon is killed without cleanup and its PID is reused, daemon stop --force can send SIGTERM and SIGKILL to an unrelated live process instead of the daemon. The pid file stores only a number and pid_alive checks existence, not process identity; the same stale record also prevents restarting the daemon. A lifetime lock plus verified process identity avoids treating recycled PIDs as daemon ownership.
findings.suggested_fix: Hold an OS lock for the daemon lifetime and bind any force-stop process reference to a verified process identity/start time; refuse to signal when ownership cannot be established.
